explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, "You understand my thoughts from afar." Your thoughts are the one room you figure nobody can walk into. The LORD doesn't need to come any closer to understand them. I think David is amazed by that, and I'd be too.

Dreams are a fair guess, friend, but this psalm never mentions them. What David says is, "You understand my thoughts from afar." Sitting and rising are what he does, and thoughts are what's going on inside him. I've had plenty of dreams about a clean kitchen counter, but the psalm doesn't go there.

David wrote psalms, so I see why songs came to mind. But the verse says something else: "You understand my thoughts from afar." It's about what goes on inside him, not what he sings. The LORD understands that part from afar.

Close, baker, but David says the opposite. He says, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD." So the LORD doesn't wait for the words to come out. He knows before David opens his mouth.

Right, baker. David says, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD." The words haven't even left his tongue yet. That's a lot of knowing, and I can't even guess what I'm about to say before I say it.

explanations.answer: He can't fully take it in
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David says, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." It's too big for him to reach. I think he's standing there amazed, like a guy staring up at the tallest oven he's ever seen.

I see why you'd think so, but that isn't what David means. He calls this knowledge "…too wonderful for me…" That's amazement, not dread. At the end of the psalm he even asks, "Search me, O God, and know my heart…"
Not quite, baker. David says this knowledge is "…too lofty for me to attain." He's admitting it's out of his reach. Honestly, that's me every time I look at a mixer with too many buttons.

That's right. David says, "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." Sheol is the realm of the dead, so he's naming the highest place and the deepest place. The LORD is there in both. That's a lot of ground covered, friend.

This one is true, friend. David says, "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." Sheol is the realm of the dead. He names the highest place and the deepest place, and the LORD is in both.
Yes, baker. David says, "…even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." So even at the farthest sea, he isn't alone out there. He gets guided and held.

Almost, friend, but this one is true. David says, "…even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." Even at the farthest sea, he gets guided AND held. That's a lot of care for one spot on the map.

explanations.answer: Night is as bright as day to God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "…even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You." So if David hoped the dark would hide him, it wouldn't. God sees there like it's noon.

explanations.answer: God simply waits for the morning
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but God isn't waiting on any sunrise. David says, "…the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You." The dark doesn't slow God down at all. I've waited on plenty of mornings myself, but God doesn't need to.

explanations.answer: David's voice always gives him away
explanations.explanation: That would be a funny reason, baker, but David never says it. His reason is, "…even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day…" It's about what God can see. David's voice doesn't come into it.

Yes, baker. David says, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Just before that, he says God formed his inmost being and knit him together in his mother's womb. He looks at how he was made and what comes out of him is praise.
That's a fair guess, friend, but David isn't asking any questions here. He says, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." What comes out of him is praise.
Going quiet makes sense, baker, since it's a big thing to think about. But David speaks up here. He says, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." He's anything but silent.

Careful, friend, because this one trips people up. David does say he was made in secret and woven together in the depths of the earth. But he also says, "My frame was not hidden from You…" So being made in secret didn't keep his frame from God.

That's right, baker. David says, "My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth." It was made in secret, but God saw all of it. No part of David was hidden from Him.
It's the other way around, friend. David says all his days "…were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." So the writing came first, before a single day began.

Correct, baker. David says, "all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." Not one of them had started yet, and they were already written down. So the book came first, and the living came after.

Yes, baker. David says, "…how vast is their sum!" and then, "If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand…" Think about counting a whole beach, and then there's still more. That's how vast God's thoughts are.
I get why you'd pick it, friend, but David isn't talking about hidden thoughts. He says, "If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand…" That's about how many, not about secrecy.
Holy is a good word, but it isn't what David says here. He says, "…how vast is their sum!" and that they "…would outnumber the grains of sand…" It's about how many thoughts there are, friend.

That's what the text says, baker. David says, "O God, that You would slay the wicked…" This is a heavy part of the psalm, and I won't dress it up. He asks it of God, and he says it with strong feelings.
I see why you'd hope so, friend, but that isn't what David asks here. He says, "O God, that You would slay the wicked…" It's a heavy verse, and he prays it with strong feelings.
That's a gentle guess, baker, but David asks for something stronger. He says, "O God, that You would slay the wicked…" It's a heavy verse, and he asks it of God.
Not this time, friend. David says these men "…speak of You deceitfully…" That means their words about God aren't honest. He also says, "Your enemies take Your name in vain."
That's right, baker. David says they "…speak of You deceitfully…" So their words about God aren't honest. He adds, "Your enemies take Your name in vain."
Yes, baker. David says, "See if there is any offensive way in me…" He asks God to look. I'd sooner hide a burnt batch under a dish towel, but David asks.
Actually this one is true, friend. David says, "See if there is any offensive way in me…" He asks God to look. That's a brave thing to say out loud.

explanations.answer: In the way that lasts forever
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, "lead me in the way everlasting." He starts the psalm with God searching him, and he ends it asking God to lead him. I think that's a good way to finish.

explanations.answer: In the way of his fathers
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible guess, friend, but David doesn't mention his fathers. He says, "lead me in the way everlasting." He's asking God to lead him in the way that lasts forever.

explanations.answer: In the way back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Jerusalem would be a nice place to be led, baker, but the psalm never says it. David asks, "lead me in the way everlasting." It's about a way that never ends, not a place on the map.
